newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Canada says WTO improves markets for LLDCs.
newsitem.headline: Canada says WTO improves markets for LLDCs.

text.p: Trade opportunities for least developed countries (LLDCs) and developing countries were taken up at the World Trade Organisation (WTO), including a proposal by Canada for a meeting to reach these objectives, Canada's trade minister said on Friday.
Art Eggleton said WTO targets included a plan of action for improving investments and market conditions for these countries.

"It also deals with a Canadian proposal that a meeting be held early in the new year....to foster an integrated approach assisting these countries in enhancing their trade opportunities," Eggleton said.
The meeting will involve the United Nation's UNCTAD, the International Trade Centre, WTO, international aid agencies and multilateral financial institutions.
Asked about tax concessions to developing countries, such as zero tariffs for textiles and clothing, Eggleton said: "That's got considerable sensitivity for Canadian domestic industry."
He added there was already an agreement on textiles and clothing, and a quota system in place.
"All countries agreed to this (paragraph 15), developing and least developed countries were involved in this," Eggleton said.
"There is an agreement on textiles and clothing and we are honouring that agreement, to change that course opens up difficulty with respect to preservation of jobs back home," the minister said.
Ministers from 128 countries on Friday formally approved a declaration pledging their governments to work for wider freedom in trade at the WTO's first ministerial meeting in Singapore.
But the talks were criticised by some for being too focused on achieving agreement on an information technology pact, and not enough on issues affecting poorer countries.

"On textiles and clothing, our assessment was below par," said Pakistan's minister for trade, Dr Mohammad Zubair Khan, earlier, adding Pakistan agreed to compromise only on assurances that improvements will be made later.
